title: Set aside
hookLine: is the soul the same as the body? the question is set aside
last: LET THE ANIMALS DRINK COOL WATER.

lines: IS THE SOUL THE SAME AS THE BODY?
cards: Some questions are so large they feel like they must come first. Before I do anything else, I need to know what I am. In the sixth and seventh long discourses, the same small story is told twice.
Two wandering ascetics, Mandissa and Jaliya, come to the Buddha at Kosambi, in a park called Ghosita's. They greet him politely, and ask a question the wanderers of that time argued over.
Is the soul the same thing as the body? Or is the soul one thing and the body another?

teach.h: JIVA AND SARIRA: SOUL AND BODY
teach.b: The Pali word for soul here is jiva: life, the living principle. Body is sarira. The Buddha doesn't say yes, and he doesn't say no.
He says: listen, and pay close attention.

teach.h: NO ANSWER, BUT A LIFE DESCRIBED
teach.b: And instead of an argument, he describes a life. A Buddha arises in the world. Someone hears the teaching and goes forth.

They keep the moral conduct, guard the senses, practice mindfulness, become content. They set down the hindrances and enter the four absorptions. Then they turn the clear mind toward knowing, and see things as they are.
Would it be fitting, he asks, for someone who knows and sees like this to say either one?

teach.h: I KNOW, I SEE, I DON'T SAY
teach.b: And of himself: I know this, I see this, and I don't say either that the soul is the body or that it's something else. That's the move.
The question isn't called stupid. It isn't answered.

It's set aside, because the training goes somewhere the question doesn't reach. We met this before, with the man struck by a poisoned arrow who wouldn't let the doctor treat him until he knew who shot it.
Here the emphasis is different. Someone who actually sees clearly no longer feels the need to put things in those two boxes.
The question was built on a frame, a self either identical to the body or separate from it, and clear seeing doesn't fit that frame. The wanderers came with a big question.
They were offered a way of living in which the question loosens its grip.

how: Buddhist schools generally treat speculative questions about the soul and body as undeclared, and teachers redirect students toward practice; how to understand the person in the absence of a fixed self is explained differently across schools.

o: put down, neither answered nor mocked
saved to be answered later on

s: the Buddha answers that the soul and body are the same
he doesn't say either; he describes the training and sets the question aside.
the same story appears in two long discourses
DN 6 and DN 7 both tell of Mandissa and Jaliya.
setting the question aside means calling it stupid
it isn't mocked; clear seeing simply goes where the question doesn't reach.

games.q: two wanderers ask you: is the soul the same as the body, or different? you're the Buddha in DN 6–7. what do you do?
o: describe the training, and say: I know and see, yet I don't say either.
games.why: he describes a whole life of practice, from going forth to clear seeing, and says that knowing and seeing this way, he doesn't take either side.

practice: Notice one big question you carry, what's the meaning of it all, what am I really, what happens after, and hold it for a moment.
Then kindly set it down beside you, like a bag you can pick up later, and be with what's here: breath, body, sounds.

wordCard.voice: Set aside. A question neither answered nor mocked, but put down, because clear seeing goes where the question doesn't reach.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit jiva: life, soul, the living principle. paired with sarira, body.

carryVoice: Your line: set it aside. The question isn't thrown away; it's resting. Day five hundred thirty-five.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 6, Mahali Sutta (to Mahali), the Mandissa and Jaliya episode
